turns.prompt_text: I would like to learn more about Google Sheets in Excel. I feel like it would help me but I'm not sure if it would actually be a practical use of my learning time and learning attention and focus.
turns.response_html:
It sounds like there might be a bit of a mix-up in terminology! Google Sheets and Microsoft Excel are actually two different, competing spreadsheet applications. While they do roughly the same thing—organize data, run calculations, and create charts—they live in different ecosystems.

Think of it like choosing between a Mac and a PC. They both get the work done, but the "feel" and specific features differ.

Is it a practical use of your time?

In short: Absolutely.

Whether you are navigating the rigors of a computer science graduate program, managing software engineering tasks, or tracking components for a DIY electronics project, spreadsheet proficiency is a "force multiplier." It allows you to move from "looking at data" to "manipulating reality."

1. The Professional Perspective (Software Engineering)

As an engineer, you might think, "I can just write a script for that." While true, a spreadsheet is often the fastest way to:

  • Analyze logs: Quickly filter and sort CSV exports.
  • Project Management: Build quick-and-dirty Gantt charts or budget trackers for contract work.
  • API Testing: Organize request/response data points before hard-coding them.

2. The Academic Perspective (Graduate Studies)

In a Master's program—especially in technical fields—you will inevitably encounter data. Using a spreadsheet to organize research citations, track experiment variables, or even manage your study schedule can save hours of cognitive load.

3. The Personal & Hobbyist Perspective

If you're into 3D printing or building custom electronics (like an EEG headset), spreadsheets are invaluable for:

  • Bill of Materials (BOM): Tracking parts, prices, and shipping statuses.
  • Calibration Logs: Recording print settings and results to find the "sweet spot" for your equipment.

Google Sheets vs. Microsoft Excel

Since you'll likely use both at some point, here is a quick breakdown of how they stack up:

FeatureGoogle SheetsMicrosoft Excel
CollaborationBuilt for it. Real-time editing is seamless.Possible via OneDrive, but can be clunkier.
PowerGreat for most tasks, but struggles with massive datasets.The "Gold Standard" for heavy data crunching.
CostFree for personal use.Usually requires an Office 365 subscription.
ScriptingUses Apps Script (based on JavaScript).Uses VBA or Office Scripts (TypeScript).
OfflinePossible, but primarily web-based.Robust desktop application; works perfectly offline.

Which one should you focus on?

Given your background in software engineering and your interest in automation (like using Google Apps Script), Google Sheets might feel more intuitive. The ability to connect it to other web services via APIs or scripts makes it a powerful tool for a developer's toolkit.

However, if you find yourself dealing with massive datasets in your graduate research or professional engineering roles, the raw processing power of Excel is unmatched.

The good news: 90% of the skills are transferable. If you learn how to write a VLOOKUP or a PIVOT TABLE in one, you know how to do it in the other.

Are you looking to use a spreadsheet for a specific project right now, or are you just looking to sharpen your general "digital utility belt"?

turns.prompt_text: I know Microsoft Excel is often touted for being very powerful, however I feel like if I need a lot of power I can just use Python or a script and I would rather have something that's more visual and intuitive like Google sheets. I also use the Google ecosystem a lot and almost never use the Microsoft ecosystem and is very annoying to me and cumbersome
turns.response_html:
It sounds like you've already hit on the most important realization: Google Sheets isn't a replacement for Python; it’s a UI for it.

As a software engineer and graduate student, your "learning time" is your most valuable asset. If Excel feels cumbersome and "Microsoft-heavy," fighting that friction is rarely productive. Given your background in DIY electronics and coding, here is why focusing on Google Sheets is a highly practical move:

1. The "Frontend" for Your Python Scripts

Since you are comfortable with Python, you don't need a spreadsheet to be a "powerhouse." You need it to be a dashboard.

  • The Workflow: Use Python (with libraries like gspread or pandas) to do the heavy lifting—cleaning 50,000 rows of sensor data from your 3D printer or analyzing logs for work.
  • The Result: Instead of printing a boring terminal output, have your script push the results to a Google Sheet. Now you have a beautiful, visual, and shareable interface that you can access from your phone or Mac Mini without running a script every time you want to see a chart.

2. The "Jarvis" Factor (New for 2026)

Google has leaned heavily into making Sheets feel intuitive through Gemini integration. This fits your preference for a "natural" learning intuition rather than memorizing rigid formulas.

  • Natural Language Queries: You can now open the Gemini sidebar and simply ask, "What was my average filament usage in March?" or "Create a pivot table of my Fareway work hours by week." It generates the logic for you.
  • The =AI() Function: You can use =AI("summarize this data") directly in a cell. This turns your spreadsheet into a thinking assistant rather than just a calculator.

3. Practicality for Your Specific Projects

Project / GoalHow Google Sheets Scales Your Time
Software EngineeringUse it as a lightweight Issue Tracker or Feature Backlog for your NeapolitanLabs contracts. It’s faster than setting up a full Jira instance.
DIY ElectronicsMaintain a Bill of Materials (BOM). You can use =IMPORTXML to live-track prices for components on electronics sites so you know exactly when to buy your next Raspberry Pi.
Graduate StudiesTrack your Research Sources. Using the Google ecosystem allows you to sync data directly from Google Scholar or Forms into a sheet for easy sorting.

4. Why Not Excel?

You’re right to skip it if the ecosystem feels like a "walled garden." While Excel recently added native Python support (letting you write Python directly in cells), it still lacks the live collaboration and web-native API feel of Google Sheets. For a developer, being able to POST data to a spreadsheet via a simple web hook is often more useful than having a 500-page manual on VBA macros.

My Recommendation

Don't try to "master" Google Sheets by memorizing every function. Instead, learn these three "Developer-First" skills:

  1. QUERY() function: It uses a SQL-like syntax that you will find much more intuitive than standard spreadsheet nesting.
  2. Google Apps Script (JavaScript): Since you know code, this will feel like a superpower for automating your Fareway schedule or 3D printing logs.
  3. Python Integration: Learn how to use the Google Sheets API to turn your Python scripts into live-updating visual tools.

Does that "frontend for your code" approach feel more aligned with how you'd actually use it day-to-day?

turns.prompt_text: So I have this other problem in that whenever I'm operating the terminal on my computer it's just a very clunky poor experience. The problem with it mainly is that the the commands have a lot of free-range power and it's difficult to see what you're doing and where. I've used terminal for years and I know a lot from a minor in cyber security from using the terminal and different operating systems such as Linux, macos, Windows. I really don't like using it and having to do all the flags and all the things and enter everything and having a rough time with them and the text editors and having to install things and make things look pretty. I would prefer some type of middleman. I would be A-Okay if an AI took a hold of it because I think in a I would even be safer than just me entering in commands
turns.response_html:
It sounds like you’ve reached the "CLI Fatigue" stage that many experienced engineers eventually hit. After years of cybersecurity and systems work, the novelty of memorizing flags for tar or grep wears off, and the risk of a typo causing a "free-range power" disaster becomes a real cognitive burden.

Since you are on a Mac and prefer a visual, intuitive ecosystem, there are "middleman" solutions that treat the terminal more like a modern IDE and less like a 1970s teleprinter.

1. Warp: The "Google Sheets" of Terminals

If you want a visual and intuitive experience without leaving the terminal entirely, Warp is the current industry leader for Mac users. It reimagines the terminal as a modern app.

  • Blocks, not Scrolls: Instead of a giant wall of text, every command and its output is grouped into a "block." You can right-click a block to copy just the output, search within it, or even share it as a link.
  • The AI "Middleman": It has a built-in "AI Command Search." You type #How do I find all files over 100MB and sort by date in plain English, and it gives you the exact command with the flags ready to go.
  • Visual Workflows: You can save complex sequences of commands as visual workflows so you don't have to remember them next time.

2. Open Interpreter: Letting the AI "Take the Wheel"

Since you mentioned being okay with an AI taking hold of the terminal for safety and ease, Open Interpreter is likely exactly what you are looking for. It is an open-source project that lets a Large Language Model (like GPT-4 or Gemini) operate your computer's terminal directly.

  • How it works: You run interpreter in your terminal, and then you just talk to it.
  • The Workflow: You say: "Find all the logs from my 3D printer project from last Tuesday, find any errors related to 'extrusion', and summarize them in a Google Doc."
  • Safety First: It doesn't just run things blindly. It shows you the code it's about to run and asks for your permission (unless you explicitly tell it not to). This acts as that "middleman" filter you’re looking for.

3. Raycast: The GUI-First Command Line

Since you find the Microsoft ecosystem cumbersome and prefer the fluid Mac experience, Raycast might be your best bet for avoiding the terminal altogether for common tasks.

  • Extensions as Commands: Instead of opening a terminal to flush your DNS or check a port, you just hit Cmd + Space, type "Flush," and hit enter.
  • Developer-Centric: There are thousands of community-built "Scripts" that provide a GUI for terminal-heavy tasks (like managing Docker containers, interacting with GitHub, or formatting JSON).
  • Visual Interface: It provides clear, visual feedback for every action, so you never have to wonder "did that command actually work?"

Why this is actually "Safer"

Your intuition that AI might be safer is backed by a solid logic: The "Intent vs. Syntax" Gap. Most terminal errors happen because your intent was correct, but your syntax (a missing flag, a misplaced slash) was wrong.

By using an AI middleman:

  1. You express the Intent in natural language.
  2. The AI translates that into Syntax.
  3. You perform a Visual Audit of the command before it executes.

This removes the "clunkiness" of the text editor and the "guesswork" of the flags.

Given your interest in building automation—like your Google Apps Script for your work schedule—would you prefer a tool that you can interact with via voice/chat (like Open Interpreter), or a redesigned visual terminal that just makes the manual typing less painful (like Warp)?

turns.prompt_text: Because I already paid for Gemini and may even upgrade. Is there a way I could pipe this into the terminal?
turns.response_html:
Since you are already in the Google ecosystem and have a Gemini subscription, you have a perfect "bridge" for your terminal frustration. In 2026, Google has released an official, terminal-native way to do exactly what you're asking.

It’s called the Gemini CLI, and it acts as the intelligent "middleman" you’ve been looking for.

The Solution: Gemini CLI (2026 Edition)

Instead of typing raw, risky commands, you can use the gemini command to handle the "syntax" while you focus on the "intent."

1. Why it fits your "Safety First" request

The Gemini CLI includes a specific feature called Plan Mode. When you ask it to do something complex, it doesn't just run the command.

  • The Plan: It generates a step-by-step list of the commands it intends to run.
  • The Review: It pauses and waits for you to hit Y to approve each step or the whole block.
  • The Guardrail: It can even run commands inside a local Docker container (sandbox) if you’re testing something particularly "free-range" or risky, keeping your actual macOS filesystem safe.

2. How to "Pipe" into it

You can treat Gemini just like any other terminal utility. Because it supports standard input/output (pipes), you can do things like:

  • Log Analysis: cat server.log | gemini "Find all the 'extrusion' errors from my 3D printer and tell me the most likely cause."
  • File Transformation: ls -la | gemini "Convert this list into a JSON format and save it to 'files.json'."
  • Code Explanation: cat script.py | gemini "Explain what the flags in this script do like I'm a cybersecurity minor."

Installation & Setup

Since you’re on a Mac and prefer the Google/Apple-friendly path over the Microsoft path, Homebrew is the easiest way to get started.

  1. Install: Open your terminal and run: brew install gemini-cli
  2. Authenticate: Link it to your existing Google account: gemini auth (This will open a browser window for a standard Google login. It will recognize your paid subscription and give you higher rate limits/access to Gemini 3 Pro).
  3. Use it: gemini "Look at my current directory and tell me which files are taking up the most space."

The "Take the Wheel" Option: Open Interpreter

If the official CLI feels too "manual," you can use Open Interpreter, which is a third-party tool that supports Gemini.

  • Autonomous Agent: This is the one that truly "takes the wheel." You give it a goal (e.g., "Clean up my downloads folder and organize everything by project name"), and it writes the code, runs the terminal commands, sees the errors, and fixes them itself until the job is done.
  • Set it to Gemini: You can run it with interpreter --model gemini/gemini-3-pro to ensure it's using the engine you’re already paying for.

My Recommendation

Start with the official Gemini CLI. It feels more like a "Google product"—polished, intuitive, and less "hacker-clunky" than the standard terminal experience. It gives you the visual feedback you want without making you feel like you're one typo away from deleting your home directory.

Which of your current terminal "headaches" would you want to hand over to this assistant first?

turns.prompt_text: Now that I'm thinking about this it would be nice to be able to get rid of the keyboard as much as possible. It certainly would be good on my shoulders and posture so that I can move everything to a microphone.
turns.response_html:
This is a significant transition, Austin, but as someone navigating both graduate-level CS and professional software engineering, it’s a move that can actually increase your throughput once the "syntax" of voice-coding clicks.

Since you’re already in the Gemini ecosystem and prefer a "Jarvis-like" assistant, here is how you can move the terminal—and your entire macOS workflow—to a microphone-first setup in 2026.

1. The "Jarvis" Core: Gemini Live + Open Interpreter

To truly get your hands off the keyboard, you need an agent that can listen to your intent and execute the terminal commands autonomously.

  • The Tool: Open Interpreter (configured to use your Gemini 3 Pro subscription).
  • The Workflow: You don't type ls -la or git commit. Instead, you speak to your Mac:

    "Hey Jarvis, look at the recent changes in my NeapolitanLabs project, run the test suite, and if it passes, push it to the 'dev' branch with a descriptive commit message."

  • Why it works: Because you’re using Gemini, it can handle the ambiguity. If the tests fail, it won’t just stop; it will read the error logs (which you hate doing manually) and say, "The build failed due to a missing dependency in line 42. Should I install it for you?"

2. The "Operating System" Layer: Wispr Flow

While Gemini handles the terminal "logic," you still need a way to control the rest of your Mac (emails, Notion, your grad school research) without a keyboard.

  • The Tool: Wispr Flow (The 2026 gold standard for Mac engineers).
  • The Experience: It’s a "zero-friction" dictation layer. Unlike the old-school Mac dictation that was clunky and required "Command-Space" to start, Wispr Flow is always listening for a specific trigger.
  • Developer-Friendly: It’s smart enough to know when you’re speaking Prose (like an email to your professor) vs. Code (like a Python snippet). It handles camelCase, snake_case, and technical terms like "React Hook" or "EEG signal processing" without you having to spell them out.

3. The Visual "Audit" (Safety & Posture)

Since your goal is to save your shoulders, you don't want to be hunched over a 13" laptop screen checking the AI's work.

  • Large Display Strategy: Since you have those LG UltraGear monitors, set one up at eye level.
  • The Setup: Keep a terminal window open running Gemini in Plan Mode.
    1. You speak the command.
    2. The "Plan" appears in large, readable text on your monitor.
    3. You simply say "Approved" or "Go" to execute.
  • The Result: You can lean back, keep your chest open, and work entirely from a high-quality microphone (like a dedicated USB condenser mic or even the high-end array in your MacBook Air).

Your 2026 "Hands-Free" Stack

TaskSoftwareHuman Action
Terminal / CodingOpen Interpreter + Gemini 3 ProNatural Language Intent
Email / Docs / ChatWispr FlowDirect Dictation
System ControlRaycast (Voice Search)"Open IntelliJ" / "Empty Trash"

A Quick Reality Check for an Engineer

The biggest hurdle won't be the technology—it’s the mental shift. You’ve spent years thinking in "flags" and "semicolons." To make this work for your posture, you have to start thinking in "Goals."

Instead of: "Open the Python file, scroll to line 50, change the variable name..." Try: "Refactor the data parser in my 3D printer script to use the new API format we discussed."

Does this sound like a setup that would actually allow you to push your keyboard aside for the majority of your day?
